title: Tenant-scoped trace filtering, access-annotations, and consent-aware retention policy
creator: Maya Chen
description: Problem: Our tracing pipeline currently retains full spans and attributes for the global default TTL. That means customer-identifying attributes (email, phone, user_id patterns) can be present in traces longer than allowed by tenant agreements or consent flags. There is no consistent hook to record consent or data-class annotations on spans emitted from the runtime and SDKs.
goal: Provide a coherent, tenant-scoped tracing governance model that: 1) allows runtime/SDKs to annotate spans with access and consent metadata at emit-time; 2) enables the pipeline to apply conditional masking or drop rules before long-term storage; 3) surfaces access events in an auditable log tied to RBAC decisions and retention changes; and 4) exposes a small set of Console controls for per-tenant retention tiers and consent toggles.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Runtime and SDKs can attach standard attributes: redwood.tenant_id, redwood.consent_level (none/opt_in/opt_out/limited), redwood.data_class set (PII/SENSITIVE/NON_SENSITIVE). 2) Ingest pipeline applies masking rules based on these attributes and a tenant-policy table. 3) Traces and derived metrics respect per-tenant retention TTLs and are removed or moved to short-term buckets when consent revoked. 4) All access by platform operators to raw unmasked traces is logged to an immutable access trail and surfaced in Console audit logs. 5) A minimal demo (trace + masking + automated TTL enforcement) is deployed to staging and validated against two tenant configs.
design_summary: We will introduce an 'access-annotation' contract inside the OpenTelemetry span attributes that the runtime and SDKs publish. The ingestion pipeline will add a policy-enforcement stage (policy-engine v2) which consumes tenant metadata (from CustomerConfig DB) plus consent tokens and applies transformation rules: drop_attributes, hash_attributes, redact_value, or drop_span. We will support both attribute-level redaction and span-level policy. Retention enforcement will be implemented by tagging traces with retention_bucket and hooking into the retention worker to sweep based on bucket TTLs. Operator access to full traces will require a justification token and be recorded in AccessLog with tenant and operator identity. Console will have a per-tenant 'observability privacy' page to surface current policies and last access events.
implementation_notes: Runtime changes: add instrumentation helpers in go/runtime and python/sdk to set redwood.* attributes. Add validation layer to reject PII in top-level event fields unless tenant policy permits. Ingest pipeline: add policy-enforcement stage as a deterministic step before long-term storage; it must be idempotent and lane-aware. Retention worker: support dynamic TTLs per trace via retention_bucket tag. Audit logging: reuse existing audit stream but add dedicated schema fields for trace_id, span_id, justification_token, operator_id, and action. Storage migration: short-term bucket (30d) and long-term bucket (13m) labels. When consent changes to more restrictive, trigger a backfill job that re-evaluates recent traces and either redacts or queues for deletion depending on policy.
api_changes: SDKs: new Optional TracingOptions struct with 'consent_level' and 'data_class' fields. Ingest API: Accept new header X-Redwood-Consent-Token for server-side signed consent assertions. Console API: endpoints to update tenant policy and to retrieve recent access-log entries.
security_and_privacy_considerations: All consent tokens must be signed with customer-specific keys and validated in policy-engine. Any unmasked trace viewing requires a just-in-time escalation and must be logged to the immutable access trail. Masking techniques must prefer deterministic hashing for identifiers when downstream debugging requires joinability; where deterministic hashing is not permitted, redact and emit an opaque pseudonym. Threat model: risk of unauthorized access by ops; mitigations include RBAC, just-in-time tokens, alerting on cross-tenant access, and periodic audits.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (staging): implement runtime annotations and pipeline policy-stage in a non-destructive mode (masking simulated, raw traces still stored) to gather false-positive rates. Phase 2 (canary): enable masking for 10% of tenants with known consent configs and monitor developer debug impact and support tickets. Phase 3 (general): flip masking for all tenants and enable retention enforcement. Each phase includes a rollback switch and an incident runbook. Console controls will be gated behind feature flags until Phase 3.
migration_and_backfill: We will run a backfill job that re-processes traces from the last 90 days into the policy-engine to either redact or tag them for deletion based on each tenant's current consent. Backfill will be rate-limited and monitored via a dedicated dashboard. A subset of critical traces (internally marked) will be excluded from automated deletion until manual review.
monitoring_and_telemetry: Create dashboards: 1) Policy hit rate by tenant and rule, 2) Masking false-positive/false-negative counts (via sample review), 3) Access-log events per operator, 4) Sweep/delete job progress and error rate, 5) Developer impact: increase in support requests referencing missing trace attributes. Add alerts for unusual bulk access or mass policy flips.
open_decisions: 1) Standardize allowed data_class vocabulary and exact attribute names (proposal: PII/SENSITIVE/NON_SENSITIVE/AGGREGATE). 2) Whether deterministic hashing is allowed by default or opt-in per tenant. 3) Retention bucket sizes and default TTLs for consent levels. 4) How to surface just-in-time justification tokens in Console and whether to support short-lived operator session tokens.
risks: 1) Over-masking could break customer debugging flows. 2) Backfill cost and rate limits might impact ingest performance. 3) Operator access UX friction could slow SRE incident response. 4) Incorrect consent token validation could leave data exposed.
mitigations: 1) Keep non-destructive simulation mode for 3 weeks and run targeted follow-ups with impacted partners. 2) Backfill will use low-priority compute and respect ingest QPS. 3) Provide a fast-path emergency escalation procedure with stricter logging and post-mortem requirements. 4) Add integration tests for consent token handling and a fuzz tester for policy-engine rules.
acceptance_tests: 1) Unit tests for SDK attribute injection, consent token validation, and policy-engine rule application. 2) Integration test that simulates a consent revocation and verifies traces are redacted or deleted within SLA. 3) End-to-end demo with two tenant configs showing different retention and masking behaviors. 4) Audit log review verification showing operator access entries.
